title: Follow one workflow run without guessing
description: Use correlated logs, routing explanations and metrics to distinguish skipped work from failed work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional operator asking why a recording never reached a custom stage. Where do we start without scrolling through a wall of unrelated logs?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find the recording's media key or trace identifier and follow the engine's structured log lines for that run. The same correlation fields connect lifecycle, routing and persistence outcomes. Your stage's own logs are separate, so carry the trace identity there too.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's more useful than searching for the camera's friendly name?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Much more precise. Include organisation and run context where available so nearby events from other work don't look like part of the same execution.

chapters.title: Completed can mean no stage matched

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our run says completed, but the stage produced nothing. Isn't that contradictory?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not necessarily. A run can complete without dispatching a stage. Inspect the dispatched and resolved counts, then the routing outcome. A condition may not have matched, or a required upstream result may not have been available.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How do we get a more specific explanation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The debug level adds per-stage routing decisions with the failing need and observed value. Use that detail to correct the condition rather than repeatedly restarting a healthy worker that was never asked to do anything.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What if the stage was dispatched but never returned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Look for the timeout warning and unresolved count, then inspect the worker. Dispatch failures, malformed results and persistence failures have distinct fault lines and counters. Metrics reveal a pattern across runs; correlated logs explain a particular recording.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Check the bounded retry and dead-letter behaviour, not just the live queue. When requesting help, provide the full relevant lifecycle and routing explanation with correlation fields, but keep credentials and unrelated sensitive payloads out of shared diagnostics. A clear run story beats a screenshot of the last error.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
